question: Recent incidents of sexual abuse against women involving the use of deepfake content, notably the case of Taylor Swift who had fake images of her spread around the world, clearly show this is a matter the European Union needs to pay closer attention to. 1.

Can the Commission clarify its role and the scope of its powers in addressing the creation, distribution and consequences of deepfake content, in particular when it involves the sexual exploitation of women?
What strategies and legislative initiatives is the Commission pursuing to prevent the creation and circulation of this type of content?
What steps does the Commission intend to take to offer support and assistance to victims of deepfake content?
answer: The Commission shares the concern about the increasing spread of deep fake sexual content featuring women. On 6 February 2024, the co-legislators agreed on the proposed Directive combating violence against women and domestic violence (1). It criminalises the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, including deepfakes, and allows for their prompt removal or blocking (2).

On 13 March 2024, the European Parliament adopted the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act (3), expected to enter into force in June 2024. The Act follows a risk-based approach and bans AI manipulative or deceptive techniques that manipulate people in a significantly harmful manner.

Providers of generative AI will also have to ensure the outputs are marked and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, as far as technically feasible. Users will need to clearly label ‘deep fakes’ that appreciably resemble people as well as AI-generated text published on matters of public interest unless the text has been subject to human review and editorial responsibility.

The Digital Services Act (4), which entered into force on 16 November 2022, also includes provisions to mitigate the risks from the creation and spread of deep fakes on online platforms operating in the EU.

Tiered due diligence obligations range from content moderation policies and notice mechanisms to complaint-handling systems, risk assessments and mitigation measures to tackle the illegal dissemination of deep fakes. Victims who suffered harm from deepfakes are covered by the Victims’ Rights Directive (5), if the harmful act constitutes a crime under national law.

Victims of online crimes will receive the necessary protection and support. The proposal for the revised Directive (6) aims to upgrade the rights of victims of crime to the societal and technological developments (7).
